exam: A 35‑year‑old with sickle cell disease presents with new‑onset fatigue and Hb 6 g/dL – what investigations differentiate acute hemolysis from aplastic crisis? — Retic count, peripheral smear for sickled cells, and viral serology; low retic points to aplastic crisis.

A patient on anti‑TB therapy develops a platelet count of 15 × 10⁹/L but no bleeding – what is the next step? — Assess for drug‑induced thrombocytopenia; stop rifampicin if suspected, monitor, and give platelet transfusion only if bleeding or count <10 × 10⁹/L.

How does chronic kidney disease cause anemia and what treatment is appropriate in a low‑resource setting? — Reduced erythropoietin production; give iron supplementation and consider erythropoietin if available, otherwise transfuse when symptomatic.

A febrile child from a malaria‑endemic area has neutrophils 0.3 × 10⁹/L – what immediate management is required? — Start broad‑spectrum antibiotics after cultures, give G‑CSF if available, and treat malaria concurrently.

What distinguishes bone‑marrow failure from peripheral destruction in a patient with pancytopenia? — Bone‑marrow biopsy shows hypocellularity vs. peripheral smear showing schistocytes or parasites; retic count low in marrow failure.
Why is NSAID avoidance important in thrombocytopenic patients? — NSAIDs impair platelet function and increase gastrointestinal bleeding risk, worsening hemorrhage.

In a pregnant woman with severe anemia, how does haematopoiesis adapt and what are safe interventions? — Placental hypoxia raises erythropoietin; give iron and folate, transfuse packed cells if hemodynamically unstable.

A HIV‑positive patient presents with persistent neutropenia; what long‑term strategy improves counts? — Initiate antiretroviral therapy to restore immune function; consider prophylactic G‑CSF if recurrent infections.
ai.title: Haematopoiesis
ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Haematopoiesis is the continuous production of blood cells from stem cells in the marrow and peripheral sites. Understanding its regulation helps diagnose cytopenias and guide transfusion decisions in low‑resource settings.

b: Red marrow is active until age 30, then shifts to axial skeleton.
In severe infection or anemia, extramedullary haematopoiesis may occur in spleen or liver.
sections.p: All blood cells arise from multipotent haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) in the red marrow. Differentiation follows a hierarchy: HSC → common myeloid or lymphoid progenitor → mature lineages.

b: Erythropoiesis → red cells; driven by erythropoietin (renal hypoxia).
Myelopoiesis → neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, monocytes; driven by colony‑stimulating factors.
Lymphopoiesis → B‑ and T‑cells; dependent on IL‑7 and thymic education.
sections.p: Regulation involves growth factors (EPO, G‑CSF, TPO) and the marrow micro‑environment. Disruption at any step produces specific cytopenias.

b: Anemia: consider iron deficiency, malaria, sickle cell, chronic disease, renal failure.
Leukopenia: HIV, TB, chemotherapy, aplastic anaemia, severe malnutrition.
Thrombocytopenia: malaria, dengue, hepatitis B, herbal toxins, sepsis‑associated DIC.
sections.p: Cytopenias are common presentations on ward rounds. Recognising the lineage affected narrows the differential and directs investigations.
